paragraphs.en: Even when shadows and reflections look convincing, the final image does not consist entirely of freshly computed answers. This episode connects virtual shadow maps and modern visibility processing to path tracing, ray reconstruction, and the different roles of DLSS. We finish with a practical framework for inspecting the resources of a rendered frame. First, where should shadow memory be allocated?

paragraphs.en: Earlier, a shadow map stored the closest depth from a light's viewpoint. A visible surface was transformed into light space and compared against that stored depth to test occlusion. Virtual shadow maps retain this fundamental question.

paragraphs.en: Allocating high resolution across an entire large region is expensive. Detailed storage for areas that are tiny on screen or completely invisible wastes memory and rendering work. Meanwhile, a small shadow close to the camera may need much denser sampling.

paragraphs.en: A page is a small piece of the larger map. Its virtual address identifies that piece, while physical memory holds its contents. Having an address does not mean every piece is resident. Our sixteen-piece map and five occupied slots illustrate this distinction.

paragraphs.en: For illustration, two directions contribute two and eight. Equal-probability sampling targets an average of five. A distribution that favors the brighter direction must still estimate the same target after correct probability weighting. These numbers are explanatory examples.

paragraphs.en: Our target is the mean of the two directions: five. Select the bright direction with probability point-eight and the dim direction with point-two. Correct each value by its original half-share divided by the new selection probability. Eight times point-five over point-eight is five. Two times point-five over point-two is also five. In this particular example, either selection returns the target.
